title: Your Brand Now Has Two Front Doors, And You’re Only Watching One
summary: AI fraud prevention is reshaping contact centers. See how brands can reduce risk and prepare for non-human interactions.
body_markdown:
AI fraud prevention is becoming a business priority as non-human interactions increase across the customer journey.


We’ve already made the case that your next customer might not be human.[AI shopping agents](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/openclaw-your-next-customer/) are starting to research, compare, and narrow options before a person ever reaches the buy button, and with Meta’s Muse,[the agentic consumer is already here](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/rise-of-the-agentic-consumer/) . That means the first impression of your brand may happen somewhere you don’t control.


That’s one front door. The other sits in your contact center.


## The Other Agent in Your Contact Center


[Agents are bringing in more legitimate customers](https://techcrunch.com/2026/04/16/ai-traffic-to-us-retailers-rose-393-in-q1-and-its-boosting-their-revenue-too/) , while another kind of non-human traffic is testing your controls rather than shopping.


[Bots are now calling contact centers at volume](https://www.pindrop.com/resources/report/the-year-trust-broke-inside-the-2025-ai-fraud-spike) , using real order numbers, partial customer data, and scripts designed to stay below refund and authorization thresholds. One $21 refund rarely raises alarms. Repeat it thousands of times, and the damage is real.


That creates a different challenge from the agentic commerce conversation. One issue is about experience: how does your brand show up when an AI shopping agent is doing the browsing and buying? The other is about detection: how do you spot a non-human caller when your systems were built around human behavior?


## Most Contact Center Controls Were Built Around Human Friction


Most contact center controls were built for human callers. Voice verification, IVR logic, and agent workflows all assume people will behave like people. They pause on security questions. They get annoyed by repeated prompts. They answer a little differently each time.


Voice bots behave differently. They answer fast, stay consistent, and often get everything right. That should be a warning sign. However, most AI fraud controls are built to catch bad answers, not flawless ones.


What’s more, there’s no established playbook… yet. Contact centers that start now, by identifying weak points in the phone channel and tightening obvious IVR probe paths, will be better prepared before this becomes everyone’s problem.


## One Friction Point. Two Very Different Entry Points.


Put these two issues side by side, and the same weakness appears. Brands have spent years building service, verification, and loyalty models around one core assumption: every interaction starts with a person addressing another one.


On one side, the cost is perception. A customer’s first experience of your brand may happen through an AI interface before a human engages directly, which is exactly why familiarity and reputation now do the work a landing page used to do. On the other hand, the cost is financial and operational. Automated fraud can move quietly through the contact center, one approved exception at a time, until the pattern becomes too large to miss.


These are operating model issues that span service journey design, contact center operations, authentication, and fraud controls.


## What Needs to Change


On the agent-as-customer side, brands need service layers that work for AI agents and humans alike. That means information is structured clearly, actions are easy to complete, and the experience holds up even when a machine is navigating on the customer’s behalf.


On the bot-as-caller side, three moves matter now:


- **Map the exposure** : Identify where your phone channel accepts real customer data with limited verification and treat those points as operational risk.
- **Define what “too perfect” looks like** : Build bot detection around speed, repetition, and consistency, not only failed authentication or wrong answers.
- **Pressure-test the thresholds** : Refund and approval limits designed for occasional human exceptions were not built for automated abuse at scale.


Delivering consistent customer experiences requires training both your customer-facing teams and your AI systems. With LLMs now frequently serving as the first point of contact, they also need the ability to identify whether they are engaging with a person or another bot and respond appropriately. Specialized training informed by human expertise can[improve bot detection performance by up to 9%](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.00371v2) , helping models learn how to recognize different types of interactions and adapt their behavior as those interactions evolve. Building this capability requires continuous testing, refinement, and optimization.


AI fraud prevention requires more than stronger controls. It demands service models, training, and detection strategies built for both human and non-human interactions.[At Concentrix, we’re already helping retail clients on both fronts](https://www.concentrix.com/industries/retail-ecommerce/) : building AI-ready service models for customers arriving through third-party interfaces and strengthening contact center fraud controls and operations before automated fraud has room to scale.
